notes.meaning: The writer looks toward God's house with deep affection, amazed by its beauty because God lives there. He calls the Lord the commander of all heavenly armies, yet rejoices that this great God welcomes worshippers into His earthly dwelling.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine understood the title's mention of winepresses as a symbol for the Church, where believers are pressed by trials in this life to produce good wine for God's storehouse.

notes.meaning: An overwhelming hunger fills the writer to stand once again in the courts of the sacred tent. His whole being, both inner heart and outer body, cries out to meet the living God rather than settling for empty ceremonies.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read the two parts of the verse as the Christian's groaning under worldly pressure followed by the joy of hope.

notes.meaning: Common little birds like sparrows and swallows build their nests and safely shelter their chicks right around God's altars. Kept away from worship, the writer envies these tiny creatures because they can rest so near the God he loves as King.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine treated the sparrow as the heart and the dove as the body, explaining that good deeds must be placed on the altar of the Church's faith to be secure.

notes.meaning: Those who live and serve daily at the house of the Lord are truly happy. Being continually close to God makes their work a constant song of praise and thanksgiving.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine applied this to the citizens of heaven, where believers will rest from works of mercy and spend eternity singing praise to God.

notes.meaning: True blessing belongs to anyone who draws strength entirely from God rather than trusting in human ability. Such people have set their hearts on the journey to draw close to the Lord.

As pilgrims travel through the dry Valley of Baca, their joyful faith turns a barren desert into a place of fresh springs. God rewards their trust by sending autumn rains to fill the water pools along the way.

Instead of growing tired on the long road, the travellers receive fresh energy at each stage of their march. Not a single true pilgrim is lost, and every one of them arrives safely before God in Zion.
The writer cries out for the Lord of hosts to hear his personal prayer. He appeals to the God of Jacob, the faithful Lord who made promises to His people and answers those who seek Him.
The psalmist asks God to look kindly on the king who shields the nation. Many Christian readers also see this as a prayer asking God to accept us for the sake of Jesus, His anointed Messiah.

differ.view: Albert Barnes held that this refers strictly to the earthly king of Israel rather than to Christ.
John Gill taught that the verse specifically asks God to look on the person, blood, and righteousness of Christ on behalf of the believer.

notes.meaning: Spending just one day worshipping in God's presence is better than a thousand days spent anywhere else. The writer would rather sit as a humble servant at the temple doorway than enjoy the luxuries of ungodly homes.

The Lord provides light like the sun and protection like a shield. He gives free favor in this life and heavenly glory in the next, never holding back what is truly good from those who walk uprightly.

differ.view: John Calvin argued that all goodness in believers flows entirely from God's free grace, leaving no room for human merit.
Adam Clarke emphasized that grace first pardons and purifies the soul, and then God gives glory to those who are fully sanctified.

notes.meaning: The psalm closes by declaring that genuine joy belongs to whoever places full confidence in the Lord. Even when believers are far from the sanctuary, faith in God gives them real peace.
